Striking moderators: type of addiction moderated inattention correlation (GD 0.288 vs internet addiction mixed with GD 0.374, Q 8.636, p 0.003); gender ratio coefficient 0.0018, p .033; data collection year predicted ADHD/non-ADHD g (0.0528, p <0.001). Count inconsistencies: section 3.1 gives 32 inattention and 31 hyperactivity effect sizes vs k = 31 and 29 in 3.3 (outlier removal may explain); 3.1 says six studies with seven effect sizes for GD/non-GD vs k = 7. extraction_notes: The full text supplied is the SSRN preprint ('Early version, also known as pre-print'; search October 21, 2021; 28 studies; N = 10761), not the 2024 published version. The screening abstract (published version) reports different data: 37 studies, 14,305 participants, search February 2023, Hunter-Schmidt random effects plus multilevel meta-analysis, IU-depression r = 0.11 [0.06, 0.16] and PIU-wellbeing r = -0.17 [-0.24, -0.10]; PIU-depression and PIU-anxiety values match. Findings were extracted from the preprint per the rules; the lead may want the published full text. Table 5 prints r (Pearson) and r+ (corrected for unreliability); r recorded. r+ values: PIU-depression 0.39 [0.30, 0.48]; PIU-anxiety 0.36 [0.26, 0.45]; IU-depression 0.16 [0.09, 0.23]; IU-anxiety 0.17 [0.07, 0.27]. The text calls the PIU-anxiety 0.36 'uncorrected', contradicting Table 5. The preprint abstract says IU-anxiety p > 0.05, but Results give p = 0.01 and Table 5 flags p < 0.05. Q degrees of freedom in the text imply fewer samples than Table 5 k for IU-anxiety (Q(5) vs k 9), IU-other distress (Q(6) vs k 9) and IU-wellbeing (Q(2) vs k 5). narrative_summary: 104 jurisdiction-wide adult surveys, 57 correlates: internet gambling had the largest association with problem gambling (OR 7.59, k 19). Attempted suicide, suicidal thoughts, anxiety, depression and alcohol or drug problems showed medium-sized associations; alcohol use was not associated (OR 1.06). Gambling activities generally showed the largest effects, socio-demographic factors the smallest.
narrative_locator: Conclusion: 'Risk factors with the largest effect sizes were generally in the gambling activity category, whereas socio-demographic factors were small.'
author_conclusion: Among frequently assessed problem gambling risk factors, gambling activities, especially continuous-play formats such as EGMs and internet gambling, have the largest effects; socio-demographic effects are small; stakeholders should prioritize larger-effect correlates in prevention and screening.

A between-outcome estimate for the overall pairing (S = 44) of 0.181 (SE = 0.019, 95% CI 0.143, 0.219, p <.001) was not recorded separately. Self-objectification and internalization of appearance ideals are recorded under the body image condition because the review treats them as body image outcomes. Model: three-level meta-analysis with REML, recorded as random effects; the longitudinal analysis model is not described separately. Longitudinal I2 values (87.01, 88.81) are called 'moderate' though high by the review's own benchmarks; both longitudinal analyses report the same Q = 45.034. Longitudinal findings are a design-based subset; recorded because the abstract presents them as a main result, lead reviewer may drop them. Publication bias text says the funnel plot 'showed no symmetry' yet concludes low risk, with Egger p = .067. Conclusion calls the aggregate relationship 'moderate' while results report small r (0.189). Search end date given as April 2024 in Methods and 'mid 2024' in the abstract. Moderators not recorded: Instagram vs all platforms ES = 0.304 overall and 0.450 for self-objectification; lower risk of bias ES = 0.228; higher female percentage strengthened associations; age (continuous) had no effect. No age-group or clinical vs community subgroup estimates (all community samples). No funding or conflict statements appear in the supplied text.

The 74% (Discussion) and 12 of 19 (63%) figures differ, apparently because the 74% does not require baseline control; denominator for 74% not stated. Single-study effects in Table 2 (e.g., Yang et al. online bullying OR = 1.61; violent media; multitasking) not recorded. ADHD to later gaming addiction: 'all studies except three' significant when controlling baseline (count with result not printed as a number). Addiction to later ADHD: four longitudinal studies, described one by one. Fig. 2 summary counts and the '33-75%' range of studies with significant between-subject associations appear only via figure, not recorded. Internal inconsistencies: Results say five studies [42, 44-47] tested within-subject effects, Discussion says only four; Hygen et al. described in text as IGD at 10 related to ADHD 2 and 4 years later, Table 2 says age 14 but not 12; Stenseng et al. reported three different ways (Table 2: ADHD at 6 not related to gaming at 8, at 8 related to gaming at 10; Results: age 6 to 8 related; age section: 6 to 10). Finding 5 quote says 'controlling for baseline levels of screen time' for a media-to-ADHD path, copied as printed. Age subgroups: authors find 'little evidence' effects stronger at a specific age; no clinical versus community comparison possible (no clinically referred samples). Sex moderation in 2 single studies only. Sensitivity analysis by rater found no systematic differences. Non-counted variables (sleep, self-esteem, life satisfaction, peer relations) appear only as mediators/moderators.

extraction_notes: Pooled values are Hunter-Schmidt weighted means of Fisher z-transformed bivariate Pearson r values, many converted from other statistics (Lenhard and Lenhard; Gilpin; Lin); no CIs, p values, heterogeneity statistics or funnel plots (SDs/SEs unavailable; only 33% of contacted authors responded). Table 2 prints 'Mean r' (unweighted: LB/PG 0.25; PG/PVG 0.21) and 'W-Mean r' (0.27; 0.21); W-Mean r recorded as the pooled effect. LB/PVG pooled W-Mean r 0.40 (6 studies, meta n 3433; total n 4941) not recorded as a finding because problem video gaming is not a counted condition (both sides online). k for LB/PG recorded as 14 studies (13 publications); Table 1 shows N/A for von Meduna et al. (2019), so fewer r values may have entered the pool. PG/PVG: 20 studies, but 'For two further studies, it was not possible to generate a standardised r value' (unclear whether within the 20); Table 1 PVG/PG column has N/A entries. Total included k and total N not stated as single figures (LB search: 23 empirical publications, 18 surveys, 14 reporting associations; Search 2: 17 additional PG/PVG surveys; Fig. 2: LB 14, PG 30, PVG 23 surveys). narrative_summary: 11 of the 19 studies found that higher problem gambling severity was significantly associated with more loot box spending, including in youth samples; all four studies focused solely on loot boxes and problem gambling found significant positive associations. Evidence for other micro-transactions (pay-to-win, multiple types) and problem gambling was limited to few studies; payment frequency appeared key.
narrative_locator: Section 4 Discussion, second paragraph: 'Overall, the present review found that the higher-rated an individual scored on scales for problem gambling, the more likely they spent more money on purchasing loot boxes.'
author_conclusion: Loot box purchasing is linked to problem gambling across varied samples, but evidence is correlational; links between other micro-transactions and problem gambling or gaming are less certain; loot boxes should be regulated as gambling and purchase frequency limited.

findings.locator: Abstract, Results (full text): 'specific inducements which reduce the riskiness or cost of gambling appear to be particularly influential ( n = 3)'

narrative_summary: Across 22 studies (narrative synthesis), sports-related gambling advertising was associated with increased gambling frequency (6 studies), expenditure (3), unplanned gambling (2), likelihood of gambling (2), sponsor product use (2) and bet complexity/riskiness (2); self-reported effects were stronger in higher-risk gamblers (7). Micro/impulse-betting studies found contrary associations; adolescent associations lost significance after controls.
narrative_locator: Abstract, Conclusions (full text): 'Exposure to sports‐related gambling advertising appears to be associated with increased gambling behaviour for a wide range of advertising media.'
author_conclusion: Sports-related gambling advertising across media appears positively associated with gambling behaviour, possibly more so in higher-risk gamblers; experimental and longitudinal evidence with health outcomes is needed, but governments might intervene on precautionary grounds.
rob_tool_used: Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT)

critical_flaws: 7: PRISMA flow gives reasons by stage only; no list of excluded studies with per-study reasons
noncritical_weaknesses: 5: titles/abstracts screened by the lead reviewer, with two reviewers each checking a random 20% and no agreement statistic; full-text selection not described as duplicate
6: data extraction not described as done in duplicate
amstar2.notes: 2: PROSPERO CRD42024509195; 'The protocol and any amendments can be found on Prospero'. 3: quantitative-only inclusion justified (qualitative work addresses mechanisms, not direct behavioural impact). 4: six databases with keywords plus citation, author and website (grey literature) searches; no expert contact; English restriction not justified (acknowledged as limitation), so PY. 9: MMAT judged suitable for the mixed experimental/observational designs (covers sampling, measures, confounding); it gives no scores. 10: Table 2 lists funding for each included study. 13: observational designs, proxy exposure measures, self-report and non-representative samples discussed when interpreting results. 14: measure heterogeneity and contrary in-play betting results discussed.

conflicts: E.M. is funded by a Wellcome Trust grant (224 852/Z/21/Z). The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.
extraction_notes: Counts come from the Abstract Results (identical in the screening abstract and full-text abstract); the review gives no per-outcome denominators, so k is null (22 studies included overall). Gambling outcomes are gambling behaviour measures (frequency, expenditure, intentions, urges, perceived impact), not gambling-disorder symptom scales, except PGSI risk-level comparisons. Counts pool all advertising media; online-specific media are digital, direct (email/text) and inducements. Contrary or null results: micro/impulse-betting studies [52, 53] found advertising exposure associated with reduced likelihood of such bets; adolescent associations [46, 49] not significant after controls; a New Zealand report [35] found very low mean likelihood of advertising-prompted betting. Reference numbers differ between Table 1 and the Results text (e.g., Browne et al. [69] in Table 1 vs EMA study [36] in text; Schottler [35] in Table 1 vs a report on traditional race marketing cited as [35] in text; Russell and Hing 2020 unnumbered in Table 1 and [54] in text). Authors note one study [40] may not have measured sports-specific advertising. Single-study percentages (e.g., 57% of sports bettors influenced by direct messaging) not recorded.

narrative_summary: Across 42 mostly cross-sectional, mostly Chinese studies, heavy SFV use (typically >=4 h/day) was consistently associated with higher inattention and impulsivity, anxiety and depression; depression appeared both as consequence (one two-wave study, boys only) and as pathway into problematic use. Body-image evidence was described as mixed but gender-sensitive. No per-outcome study counts given; certainty low to very low.
narrative_locator: Conclusion: 'high exposure to SFVs is frequently associated with less favourable mental-health indicators among young people'
author_conclusion: Provisional, mostly cross-sectional evidence links heavy short-form video use in youth to attention problems, poorer working memory, higher anxiety and depression, weaker self-regulation and addiction-like use; certainty low to very low; longitudinal studies and trials needed.

extraction_notes: The beta values are stated only in the abstract, as approximations (β ≈), with no description of how they were derived; the Discussion says the review reports 'model-based estimates from individual studies', so they may be representative single-study coefficients rather than pooled values (body text gives e.g. depression β = 0.472 and anxiety β = 0.404 from one Greek study [44]). Recorded as review-level summary figures; lead reviewer to decide. Inattention and impulsivity recorded under ADHD as symptom dimensions (judgment call). N: abstract N = 46,912 vs Results 'cumulative N = 29,600' (quantitative samples); body value recorded. Records: abstract 1,498 vs Methods 1,864 vs Results 1,842. Internal citation errors: P300 EEG study cited as [36] and [37]; Discussion cites [39] for depression following addiction in boys (Results cite [49]); max sample stated as 3,036 but a 3,808-pupil study is included. Supplement numbering inconsistent (characteristics called S4, listed as S5_result_matrix). Single-study figures not recorded: reels as risk factor for positive ADHD screening (Exp B = 1.493); body-image studies. Non-counted outcomes not recorded: stress (β ≈ 0.32), addiction symptoms (β ≈ 0.60), working memory (β ≈ -0.75), self-regulation (β ≈ -0.45), loneliness, flourishing, resilience, anger (null), self-concept clarity, academic performance, bedtime procrastination.

narrative_summary: Of the included studies (stated as 4, elsewhere 6), one found digital media use (short video reels) linked to later ADHD symptoms and three found ADHD symptoms predicted later Facebook addiction, internet addiction or problematic mobile phone use. author_conclusion: Excessive digital media use, especially social media and online gaming, is positively associated with ADHD symptoms in adults, with some evidence of bidirectionality; causal direction remains uncertain, and more longitudinal research and targeted interventions are needed.

Mostly community/online gamer samples; special groups: ASD (2), IGD (3), transgender adolescents (1), disabled players (1), unemployed (1). 72.2% male; many countries.

narrative_summary: Escapist motivation (EM) for gaming was positively associated with social anxiety (1 article), psychological distress (3), gaming disorder/addiction tendency (6) and gaming impact on daily activities (8). Autistic adults reported higher EM than controls (1 article); disabled players described gaming as escape from disability-related difficulties (1 interview study). Abstract notes EM mitigated loneliness in anxious individuals.
narrative_locator: Discussion: 'Based on the aggregated results, it can be inferred that EM has a negative correlation with mental health outcomes'
author_conclusion: Escapist motivation for virtual gaming correlates with negative, maladaptive mental health, social and gaming outcomes, though causality is unconfirmed; escapism can also bring benefits such as belonging, confidence, avatar representation and less loneliness in anxious individuals.

narrative_summary: Most studies reported a significant association between sports betting (including online and fantasy sports) and problem gambling, though not all. Substance use and other behavioral addictions among sports bettors ranged from 22.1% to 71.2% across three studies. Problem sports betting was linked to male sex, younger age, impulsivity and psychological distress. All 54 studies cross-sectional.
narrative_locator: Results, Problem and Disordered Gambling Severity: 'A significant association between sports betting and problem gambling was reported in most studies'
author_conclusion: Many studies link sports betting with problem gambling; impulsive males bet more often and are more likely to have gambling problems; co-occurring substance and behavioral addictions are reported; findings are a first step toward identifying at-risk individuals.

Grant number discrepancy: front matter RTI2018-101837-B-100 vs funding statement PDI2021-124887OB-I00. Sports betting exposure includes offline/venue betting and sports lottery, not only online. narrative_summary: Across 38 cross-sectional studies, 40 of 42 statistical tests (95.24%) found significant positive associations between gambling-like activities and gambling: loot boxes 20 (95.24%), esports 14 (93.33%), skin betting 5 (100%), token wagering 1 (100%); effects mostly small to medium. author_conclusion: Gambling-like activities (loot boxes, esports, skin betting, token wagering) are generally positively associated with gambling and gaming, including problem gambling and gaming, with small-to-moderate effects; because evidence is cross-sectional, longitudinal research with representative, diverse samples is needed.

amstar2.notes: Item 1 N: RQs and inclusion criteria name exposure (GLAs) and outcome (gambling/gaming) but no population or comparator. extraction_notes: Scoping review; no pooled estimates, so cross-study counts recorded. Counts mix 'statistical tests' (overall 40 of 42) and 'studies'; for loot boxes (20, 95.24%), esports (14, 93.33%), esports betting-problem gambling (six) and risky loot box use (two) the denominator is not printed, so k left null (not computed from percentages). Conclusion gives 95.2% (gambling) and 87.0% (gaming) versus 95.24% and 86.96% in Results; Results values recorded. Effect-size tallies for GLA-gambling: loot boxes 6 small, 8 medium, 4 large; esports 3 small, 4 medium, 1 large; skin betting 1 small, 2 medium, 1 large; token wagering 1 small. GLA-gaming results (23 tests, 20 (86.96%) positive; loot boxes 10 (83.33%), esports 8 (88.89%), skin betting 1 (100%), token wagering 1 (100%)) not recorded because gaming disorder is not a map condition row (treated as online side). 'Five studies compared gambling behaviors among esports bettors and non-esports bettors' but only three studies are cited. Search yield stated as 2,437 (abstract) and 2,138 (Data extraction section). Single-study results not recorded: Marchica et al. (esports betting indirectly linked to internalizing problems such as depression and anxiety); Richard et al. (esports bettors reported more substance use and mental health symptoms). Outcomes outside the condition list mentioned but not recorded: mental/psychological distress, impulsivity, positive and negative mood, well-being. Discussion cites two later longitudinal loot box studies outside the review. Moderators noted by the review (not recorded): time-limited items, free loot boxes, near misses, cash-out and trading strengthened the loot box-gambling link.

(2023)' with 12-month follow-up, while Table 3 lists Wartberg et al. (2025) with three-year follow-up. extraction_notes: Titled a systematic review but reports a random-effects meta-analysis (Comprehensive Meta-Analysis 4.0); classified as meta-analysis. The only pooled estimate combines depression and anxiety symptoms; Q df = 21 for an analysis of '15 studies' indicates more effect sizes than studies (dependent effect sizes apparently treated as independent); no separate pooled estimate for depression or for anxiety, so per-condition vote counts are recorded as supplementary findings. 'Negative associations' (two depression, three anxiety studies) is the review's wording; unclear whether inverse or non-significant. Results use strict inequalities (0.129 < r < 0.45; 0.167 < r < 0.385); Discussion and Conclusion say 'ranging from 0.129 to 0.45' and '0.167 to 0.385'. Authors call r = 0.212 'moderately' significant. PSMU prevalence 22.4 to 23.7% (three studies) is online side only and not recorded as a finding; global prevalence figures cited from another meta-analysis not recorded. The I2 bands quoted overlap (moderate 30-60%, substantial 50-90%). Effect sizes reported as higher in academic, high-stress settings (narrative). Mediators and outcomes outside the condition list (stress, generalized trust, perceived social support, fear of COVID-19, COVID-19 misunderstanding, loneliness) not recorded. Three studies linked social media addiction with time spent or visit frequency (0.286 < r < 0.583), online-online, not recorded. Tables 1-3 and Figs 1-3 not reproduced in the text. Most included studies rated fair quality.

narrative_summary: Emotional factors (psychological distress, anxiety, depression, stress) were the second most influential driver of doomscrolling after intensity of use; doomscrolling was also described as linked to higher stress, anxiety and depression and lower well-being. No counts of studies or synthesized effect sizes were reported.
narrative_locator: Results and Discussion, p. 14104: 'psychological distress, anxiety, and depression play an important role in encouraging individuals to continue consuming news or negative content'

narrative_summary: Across four independent samples, doomscrolling consistently predicted more rumination, psychological distress, existential anxiety and secondary traumatic stress and lower work engagement; all effects were significant and in the same direction. No study examined doomscrolling in manufacturing; bridge studies linked problematic internet use and deviant cyberloafing to poorer safety behaviour.
narrative_locator: 5. Discussion and conclusion, p. 359: 'Across four independent samples, doomscrolling was consistently found to predict greater rumination, psychological distress, and existential anxiety'
author_conclusion: Doomscrolling consistently predicts rumination, distress and existential anxiety in working adults with a large descriptive effect; with bridge evidence on PIU, cyberloafing and safety it may be an occupational hazard, but the proposed model is hypothesis-generating and untested in manufacturing.

extraction_notes: Recorded d = 0.88 (headline in abstract and conclusion); the underlying printed weighted mean is β = 0.403 (Σn = 1660), from Satici 2023 psychological distress β = 0.43 (n 460), Shabahang 2024 Iran existential anxiety 0.38 (n 620), Shabahang 2024 USA 0.33 (n 180), Taskin 2024 secondary traumatic stress 0.44 (n 400); k = 4 samples from 3 studies. Authors call it a descriptive, not meta-analytic, estimate; conversion applies an r-to-d formula to regression betas from different models, and the subgroup mixes distress, existential anxiety and secondary traumatic stress. Inconsistencies: stream 2 said to have n = 5 studies but Table 4 lists 4 studies; country counts (Turkey 3, Iran 1, USA 1, UK 1) sum to 6; Yildiz & Yildiz 2025 appears in both Table 3 and Table 5, so tables show 14 unique studies against 16 stated; text says all effects run in the 'negative' direction while Table 4 shows positive effects on distress and anxiety; work engagement printed as γ = 0.16 although described as predicting worse engagement (sign possibly lost in extraction of the table). Single-study figures not recorded (existential anxiety β 0.33 to 0.38 from one study's two samples; trait anxiety pathway moderators resilience β = −0.12, intolerance of uncertainty β = 0.29). Outcomes not recorded: rumination, work engagement, life satisfaction, mental wellbeing, mindfulness, safety behaviour. Sharpe et al. 2026 scoping review counted as an included study (possible overlap).

narrative_summary: Across 47 cross-sectional studies, health anxiety (19 studies) was predominantly positively and significantly associated with cyberchondria. OCS, somatic and depressive symptoms were associated with higher cyberchondria in 19 studies; 40 studies reported positive associations with anxiety, anxiety sensitivity, hypochondria and other constructs. COVID-19 anxiety was consistently associated, except one study.
narrative_locator: Section 3.2.1.2 Cyberchondria and Psychological Risk Factors; 'obsessive–compulsive symptoms, somatic complaints, and depressive symptoms, were consistently associated with higher levels of cyberchondria in 19 studies'
author_conclusion: Cyberchondria is a compulsive behaviour of excessive, repeated online medical searching driven by health worry that further raises anxiety; main antecedents are obsessive–compulsive and depressive symptoms, anxiety, anxiety sensitivity and intolerance of uncertainty; evidence is methodologically limited.

Age: 6 studies (3 negative, 3 nonsignificant); gender: 2 higher in females, 2 nonsignificant. Disability due to an illness or health problem appears as an outcome in one study [45]. Non-counted outcomes: quality of life, wellbeing, distress, loneliness, self-esteem, personality traits, stress. Mainly Pearson correlations; effect sizes only in supplementary Table A1 (not in file). 19 of 47 studies carried over from Zheng et al.; 239 records excluded at screening because full texts could not be retrieved.

narrative_summary: Several cross-sectional studies found weak-to-moderate positive correlations between extent of OHR and health anxiety; health anxiety related to greater distress after OHR and more post-OHR doctor visits. One longitudinal study suggested reciprocal effects in low health anxious people. The one study controlling for generalised anxiety and depression found no association. No counts of studies given.
narrative_locator: Summary, Discussion and Conceptual Integration (also 'Extent of OHR'); 'extent (i.e., frequency and/or duration) of OHR correlates consistently with health anxiety'
author_conclusion: Health anxiety is associated with more frequent self-reported online health research, more distress after it, and more doctor visits afterwards; OHR can reassure or alarm and become compulsive, and a model separating problematic from compulsive OHR is proposed.

population_notes: Human users of conversational AI, any age, clinical and non-clinical; of 60 sources mapped, 28 targeted no specific population, 19 general adult or consumer samples, 6 clinical or mixed clinical/non-clinical, 4 adolescent and student, 3 other groups (teachers, mental health professionals); 24 countries, US (14) and China (12) largest.
primary_designs: Of 60 sources mapped in Table 1: quantitative surveys and experimental designs 23 (38%), evidence syntheses 13 (22%), theoretical or conceptual analyses 13 (22%), commentaries, editorials and other non-empirical 8 (13%), mixed-methods 2 (3%), qualitative interview 1 (2%)
narrative_summary: No cross-study counts for any mapped condition. Thematic synthesis of 46 studies suggests emotional reliance on AI chatbots with addiction-like features (proposed GAID); adolescents and lonely, socially anxious or depression-prone users appear more vulnerable; psychiatric patients may experience false companionship and social withdrawal; one suicide case linked to a companion chatbot; AI-induced psychosis hypothesized.
narrative_locator: Section 1 Introduction (also Sections 6, 9 and 10); 'at greater risk of developing exclusive affective relationships with AI chatbots, particularly those more prone to depression, anxiety, and loneliness'
author_conclusion: Emotional reliance on AI chatbots is an emerging clinical phenomenon with addiction-like features, particularly affecting adolescents and lonely or socially anxious people; it needs diagnostic criteria, screening tools, interventions, ethical design guidelines and longitudinal and neurobiological research.

extraction_notes: Umbrella review (systematic review of meta-analyses) with narrative synthesis; the umbrella authors converted all effect sizes (d, OR, Fisher z, Hedges g) to Pearson r and report medians and ranges by category, so recorded estimates are medians of meta-analytic r values, not pooled estimates; ranges put in labels, not CIs. Several median categories mix counted conditions with non-counted variables (moral disengagement; anger, hostility, behavioural problems; aggression, conduct problems, risky sexual behaviour). Individual meta-analysis estimates (e.g., Abregu-Crespo et al. on children with neurodevelopmental/psychiatric conditions, the disability-relevant source; John et al. on self-harm) appear only in forest plots Figs 3-7 and were not extracted. Table 3 lists hyperactivity and specific learning disorders as psychological predictors but no separate estimates are given. Non-counted outcomes: positively valenced psychological variables incl. life satisfaction, self-esteem, empathy (median r = -0.150), school-related outcomes (median r = 0.14), stress and loneliness. Internet use/internet addiction as predictor of victimization (median r = 0.19, range -0.11 to 0.87) and interventions (median r = -0.07) not recorded (no counted condition). Only two quantitative studies tested contagion, with contradictory results (Arendt et al. found exposure predicted self-harm and suicidality one month later; Brown et al. 2018 found no clustering). Quality: 8 high, 5 medium, 2 low (CASP). Seko and Lewis (2018) hopeful images: Table 2 'n = 21' vs text '32 of 86 images'. Mood decline, hopelessness and reasons for living are non-counted outcomes. Participants in 11 studies already self-harming, so harmful effects may be overstated (authors' caveat).

narrative_summary: 38 studies: 17 on effectiveness, 28 on experiences. Online peer support was associated with declines in depressive symptoms, anxiety, suicidal ideation, NSSI and self-harm, especially with professional involvement and moderation; no negative clinical outcome was reported. Experiences were mixed: self-injury communities could normalize self-harm through toxic competition; misinformation, invalidation, privacy breaches and cyberbullying were concerns.

author_conclusion: Online mental health peer support showed positive effects on clinical and personal recovery outcomes for young people, but experiences were mixed and shaped by safety, anonymity and peer interaction quality; integration with traditional services and safeguarding are recommended.

Motivation counts use k = 15 ('In 15 of the 24 included studies, statements were made about the motivations'); unburdening (5), seeking justice (4) and educate (4) not recorded; informing others and commercial goals single-study. Eight studies described disclosure messages containing mental health effects (PTSD, anxiety, depression, self-mutilation), with prevalence between 33% and 58% in two studies (message content, not recorded). Positive effects (relief of mental health problems) come mainly from one interview study (Gundersen & Zaleski). Over half of online disclosers had never disclosed before (three studies by Webber and colleagues; not recorded). 26 articles merged into 24 studies. Text is the author accepted manuscript. extraction_notes: No findings recorded: the review gives no pooled, median, range or study-count result; risk factors are listed narratively with citations only. Review type: authors call it a 'descriptive systematic overview' (Grant & Booth typology) chosen in preference to a systematic review; coded 'other review', though it could be read as a systematic review without meta-analysis (systematic search, duplicate screening, narrative synthesis, no quality appraisal). Map cell psychosis and schizophrenia: neither term appears anywhere in the text; possible misassignment. Depression, anxiety, PTSD and trauma appear as risk factors for disordered gambling (direction: condition linked to gambling); veterans section notes one study (Biddle et al., 2005) found no significant relationship between problem gambling and PTSD, anxiety or depression; older adults: at-risk/problem gambling associated with subsequent generalized anxiety and substance use disorders (Pilver et al.). Other counted conditions mentioned: ADHD scores and learning disorders (youth), traumatic brain injury (veterans), Parkinson's medication (discussion), suicide attempts more likely from Maori disordered gamblers, mental disabilities (Native Americans). k=257 from PRISMA figure ('Articles included in overview (n=257*)'); per group Youth 100, Older 32, Women 47, Veterans 12, Indigenous 40, Prisoners 18, Poverty 23; asterisk says total is less than the sum because some articles cover more than one group. PRISMA: records screened on title n=6718, excluded title/duplicate n=2398, screened for eligibility n=4320, full text excluded n=4048. Search from inception to 31 December 2018 in EBSCO (Academic Search Complete, CINAHL Plus, PsycARTICLES, PsycINFO) and PubMed (MEDLINE); risk-factor studies restricted to 2000 onwards post hoc. Social comparison, quality of interactions, social support, connectedness, network size and problematic use themes give citations but no study counts, so only narrative. Single-study prevalence of Facebook addiction (41.9% of adolescents) not recorded. Well-being outcomes (loneliness, self-esteem, life satisfaction, negative affect) outside the condition list. Search end date inferred from publication window (January 2005 to June 2016); 302 full texts reviewed, 9 excluded for bias; Multimedia Appendices 1-2 not in text.

narrative_summary: No pooled association or study counts given. Narrative synthesis: several studies linked problematic or more frequent TikTok use with higher depression and anxiety symptoms, and depression/social anxiety predicted problematic use; one study found no direct anxiety-TikTok correlation. One longitudinal study linked weekly TikTok use to hazardous drinking and problem gambling; another linked TikTok use to lower body image scores.

author_conclusion: TikTok use is associated with anxiety, depression and procrastination; age, usage patterns, neuroticism, self-control and platform design contribute to problematic use. Evidence is mostly self-reported and cross-sectional, so longitudinal research and digital literacy interventions are needed.

Total participants given as 11 462 in Abstract/Results/Discussion but 11 062 in the Conclusion. The abstract's '67.3% of such cases found among female university students' is a single-study (Smith et al.) sample figure. Map cell 'Disability general' is not addressed by the review beyond mental health symptoms.

findings.locator: Section 3.3 Meta-analysis for mental health outcomes, Table 2, row 'Overall', column 'Moderate - Severe' with 95% CI: 'Overall 1395 39.1% (36.7%-41.6%)'; heterogeneity '( I 2 = 17.3%, Q ( df = 2) = 3.00, p = .223)'

narrative_summary: Increased COVID-19 news consumption was associated with a decline in mental health in 11 studies (of 13 included); negative effects were more consistent for news obtained on social media, with mixed results for traditional media. narrative_locator: Abstract, Results (echoed in Section 4 Discussion): 'Increased consumption of COVID-19 news was associated with a decline in mental health ( n = 11).'
author_conclusion: The literature supports an association between greater COVID-19 news consumption and poorer mental health in young people, more consistently for social media news; misinformation may contribute. Longitudinal designs, EMAs and validated news-consumption measures are needed.

body image (body dissatisfaction, internalization of the thin ideal)
online_exposures: engagement with body image-focused / appearance-related content
population_notes: Individuals aged 25 or younger (children, adolescents and young adults); global literature; mostly non-clinical samples, with qualitative studies including patients with eating disorders; countries not reported.
last_search_date: December 2025 (end of the publication window, January 2019 to December 2025; exact search date not stated)
primary_designs: 45 cross-sectional, 5 longitudinal, 8 qualitative, 4 systematic reviews
narrative_summary: No counts reported. Across designs, more social media time and engagement with body image-focused content were consistently associated with body dissatisfaction, thin-ideal internalization and disordered eating; longitudinal studies attributed this to internalization and upward comparison rather than exposure itself. Photo-based platforms and problematic use were linked to disordered eating; algorithm-driven appearance content had mixed effects on eating disorder recovery.
narrative_locator: Abstract, Results: 'there was consistent evidence that greater time spent on social media and engagement with body image-focused content were associated with greater body dissatisfaction'
author_conclusion: Social media's impact on eating disorder symptoms and body image in young people depends heavily on content type, engagement style and individual vulnerability; interventions should prioritise media literacy, address appearance-focused content and strengthen protective factors.
rob_tool_used: Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and 'standardized quality checklists' (plus PRISMA guidelines), as stated in the abstract

extraction_notes: The file is labelled 'full text', but the full text is a BJPsych Open supplement page of RCPsych conference abstracts (reviewed by the RCPsych Academic Faculty, not peer reviewed by BJPsych Open). The review's own text is identical to the screening abstract; interleaved text about self-injurious behaviour in intellectual disability (Pakistan), clozapine sudden cardiac death, the LUMEN dementia AI project, and ADHD skills training belongs to other abstracts and was not used. Treated as abstract only. No study counts or effect sizes reported. Abstract says 'past six years' while the window is January 2019 to December 2025. Sex differences reported (boys binge eating; girls restrictive eating and body dissatisfaction) are not age or clinical subgroups. Lower self-esteem is a non-counted outcome. Four included systematic reviews may overlap with the primary studies.

amstar2.notes: Scoping review rated against systematic review standard. Item 1 Y: population, exposure and outcomes defined, comparator implicit. Item 4 PY: 3 databases, full PsycINFO strategy (S1 Fig), reference lists hand-searched; grey literature excluded and English/2016-2021 limits not justified. Item 6 Y: one reviewer extracted and the other independently verified all entries (judgment call). Item 13 Y: moderate quality and cross-sectional designs discussed when interpreting results. No meta-analysis, so items 11, 12, 15 NA.

funding: The authors received no specific funding for this work.
conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.
extraction_notes: No pooled estimates; counts recorded as stated. k left null where the review did not say how many studies examined the result (frequency, platforms, fitspiration experiments, body image 33, mental health 5). Time: besides the 2 direct associations, 3 cross-sectional studies found time associated with body image dissatisfaction via social comparison and thin ideal internalisation. Fitspiration result given as percentages (50% supported, 25% partly, 25% refuted of 8), recorded as 'other: percentage of studies'. Not recorded (moderators/mediators): gender 14 of 18 significant, high BMI 3 of 5, pre-existing body image concerns 4, ED risk 5, social media literacy 3, thin/fit ideal internalisation 11 of 12 (92%), self-objectification 6. Single-study figures not recorded (96% followed thin ideal, 86% met ED criteria, 71%/65% depression/anxiety symptoms; 49% orthorexia; 97% said social media hampered recovery; 17.7% of fitspiration followers at risk of ED; 51.7%/45% meal skipping). Outcomes outside the list not recorded: low mood (n = 4), body esteem, self-esteem, psychological distress, negative mood. Search run May 2021, updated 20 July 2021; publication window January 2016 to July 2021. Quality: 28 quantitative studies moderate; 4 qualitative high. Framework author spelled both 'Rodgers' and 'Rogers'. Population mixes adolescents and young adults (10-24), coded 'adolescents'.

Orthorexia mapped to the eating disorders row (authors note it is not a classified ED); muscle dysmorphia mapped to body dysmorphia (a specifier of body dysmorphic disorder). extraction_notes: Source text is a two-column PDF extraction with interleaved columns and the reference list left in; quotes were reassembled across column breaks and de-hyphenated. Total N not reported. Where n is recorded for a count finding it is the n the review gives, which for body dissatisfaction (5469) and compulsive overeating (9,068) covers only the positive studies. Not recorded: sex/gender subgroups (mixed evidence from 3 studies each for body dissatisfaction and depressive symptoms; 3 Australian studies with DE in both sexes); mental health-diet associations (body dissatisfaction-DE 5 studies, n = 2,273; DE with depressive symptoms and anxiety 2 studies, n = 1819); single influencer study (Caner); other DE manifestations (limited or no evidence from 3 studies; e.g., orthorexia OR 5.49 for nutrition posts); single-study estimates. No age subgroup analysis possible (authors). Map cell 'Disability general': PROGRESS-Plus disability dimension had no data. Apparent errors in the paper: Kleppang ORs below 1 (0.65 [0.62–0.68], 0.70 [0.68–0.73]) described as significant positive; Wilksch ORs below 1 (e.g., 0.21 [0.06–0.82]) described as greater likelihood; several Lonergan ORs with CIs that exclude the estimate (e.g., 1.04 [0.02–0.060]); Lonergan n printed as 4290 and 4209; Adiba n as 81 and 82; Caner n as 1383 and 1363; 'social media addition' typo.

primary_designs: not reported as counts; high-level evidence targeted (meta-analyses, systematic reviews, RCTs n > 50, controlled-cohort studies n > 50, population studies n > 500); Discussion notes many cross-sectional studies
narrative_summary: No pooled estimates or study counts. Section summary: thin-ideal exposure via traditional or social media is associated with greater ED risk, males and females equally. Single studies: appearance-focused social media linked to higher ED symptoms (AN sample); excessive social media use to AN and BN risk; cyberbullying predicted AN, BN, EDNOS onset; pro-ED websites reduced calorie intake.
narrative_locator: Results, section 8 Body image and social influence, Media, social media, and the internet; Summary: 'Exposure to the thin ideal via either traditional media or social media is associated with greater risk of an ED'
author_conclusion: Eating disorders have multiple risk factors (genetic, biological, childhood adversity and trauma, comorbid mental health conditions, sociocultural factors including appearance-focused social media); further research is needed to establish whether these factors are causal.

extraction_notes: Rapid narrative review, classed as other review. All online-related figures are single included studies, not recorded: pro-ED website exposure reduced calorie intake by 20% [308]; up to 25% of pro-AN forum participants male [309]; meta-analysis of idealised images found a small non-significant increase in body dissatisfaction [302]; cyberbullying predicted AN, BN and EDNOS onset [176]; excessive social media use linked to AN/BN risk and video gaming to BED [307]. Many associations between EDs and other conditions (ADHD three-fold risk, depression, anxiety, OCD, bipolar, PTSD, autism) are condition-condition, not online, so not recorded. Cross-reference errors: text says online content is discussed in 'Sect. Gender' (it is in section 8), and section summaries cite reference numbers ([270–283], [292–307]) that do not match the studies cited in those sections. Discussion says observational studies were excluded, which conflicts with inclusion of cohort and population studies. Outcomes outside the list: self-esteem, quality of life.

findings.label: More time on social media linked to higher ON symptoms irrespective of platform (positive), count of studies
findings.locator: Results of included studies, Duration of social media use: 'four studies have shown that people who spend a lot of time on social media have higher ON symptoms irrespective of the type of platform'

narrative_summary: No meta-analysis; 31 mostly cross-sectional studies. Image-based platforms (Instagram, YouTube, Tumblr) showed stronger ON associations than text-based ones; four studies found more time on social media linked to higher ON irrespective of platform; diet, fitness and nutrition content showed the strongest associations; recovery communities had mixed effects. Authors describe the relationship as bidirectional.
narrative_locator: Discussion, ON and duration of social media use (also ON and social media platforms; Table 3): 'The duration of social media use was consistently associated with ON in the included studies'
author_conclusion: A bidirectional relationship exists between ON and social media use, shaped by platform characteristics, duration of use, content themes and individual factors; longitudinal, experimental and qualitative studies in culturally diverse samples are needed.

amstar2.notes: Item 1: PICO/PECO format used. Item 2: OSF registration a priori; planned meta-analysis dropped with stated justification (heterogeneity). Item 4: five databases, grey literature, expert contact, listservs, citation search, no language or date limits, strategy validated by an information specialist, last search within 24 months. Items 5 and 6: independent duplicate screening and extraction. Item 9: MMAT 2018 applied to all designs. Item 13: high risk of bias in 15 studies, cross-sectional designs and self-report discussed.

extraction_notes: Scoping review with narrative synthesis; planned meta-analysis not done. Count denominator unclear: Results cite four studies [27, 29, 41, 44] for duration, Discussion cites six [29, 33, 41, 47, 50, 53] as consistently associated, and nine studies are said to focus on duration; k left null. Single-study figures not recorded, including contrary results: Instagram users had lower ON risk among gay men (OR=0.479, 95%CI, 0.279–0.822); social media use not associated with ON in pregnant women (Issa); Grindr OR=5.312; nutrition content OR: 5.49 in adolescents. Several correlations are printed negative (Kardaş r = −0.116; Turner r = −0.10; Özkefeli Hamurcu r = −0.11; Sener rho =−0.187) while text describes positive associations, probably reverse-scored ORTO. Yilmazel 2020 'being a woman' aOR=0.51 although text says women are at higher risk. 15 studies rated high risk of bias, yet authors call quality adequate and the evidence valid. Table 2 heading labels the qualitative appraisal as quantitative. Outcome outside the list: loneliness (partial mediator).

Erotomania (delusional, psychosis-spectrum; 5 papers with 7 case studies; 4 of 5 papers reported ideas of reference about the love object's online posts) left out because of the 12-finding cap. Depression and anxiety deliberately not reviewed. Cited external meta-analysis (Ioannidis et al.: eating disorders linked to problematic internet use) not recorded. Disability general: Mazurek et al. 2012 and Begara Iglesias et al. 2019 compared ASD with speech/language impairment, learning disability and intellectual disability groups (single-study figures, not recorded). Internal inconsistencies: 'Taken together, all four papers indicate' follows a list of 5 + 3 + 1 studies; schizotypy text says 3 of 5 positive but later 'only one out of three available studies directly tested'; Mittal 2007/2013 reference numbers differ between text and Table 3; autism text gives 65% and 96% vs Table 6 64.5% and 96.2%; Paulus et al. cited as [219] and [220]. 18 papers not retrievable at full text. Search, screening and extraction by one author. Many findings come from supplementary tables not in the text file.

extraction_notes: Classified as 'other review': narrative review with a structured database search and data extraction form, not labelled systematic, no PRISMA flow, no quality appraisal; could be argued as a systematic review without meta-analysis. No cross-study counts or pooled figures stated, so no findings recorded. Cited external meta-analysis (Rodgers et al. 2015: 9 studies, small to large effect of eating disorder website exposure on eating pathology) not this review's own result, not recorded. Depressive symptoms appear only in a single study (Tiggemann and Slater 2015); anxiety only as a state outcome in one experiment (Mabe et al. 2014); negative mood, self-esteem and well-being outcomes not recorded. Design counts as printed (36, 20, 8, 6) may not reconcile with 67 included studies; lead reviewer to check. 52 of 67 studies collected data, sample sizes 17 to 2036. Map cell 'Benefit and support': review notes support functions of pro-eating disorder communities and calls for research on positive body image, no data. Text appears scraped from the publisher web page (includes 'Similar content' links); Table 1 and declarations not reproduced.

Intensity of use was positively associated with depressive symptoms in 6 of 10 studies and anxiety in 4 of 9; disordered eating in 5 of 7. narrative_summary: Of 43 experiments, 38 assessed body dissatisfaction: viewing attractive and thin idealized SNS images consistently increased women's body dissatisfaction versus neutral or realistic images (small to large effects); fitspiration effects were mixed in women but negative in men. Body appreciation decreased in only 1 of 8 studies. Body-positive content: mixed, 2 of 4 studies found captions ineffective.

author_conclusion: Viewing SNS images of unattainable thin, attractive and fit ideals causes short-term body dissatisfaction in young women (and fitspiration in men), with appearance comparison central; body-positive content shows preliminary promise; adolescents and long-term effects need study.

extraction_notes: Narrative synthesis of experiments; no pooled estimates. Range findings recorded with estimate null; the range bounds appear in label and locator and are not confidence intervals, so ci fields are null. Not recorded per subgroup rule: men (fitspiration ηp2 = 0.03; d = 0.90; multiple exposure to attractive images no effect). Not recorded (mediation/moderation): state appearance comparison mediated effects in 4 studies (β = 0.05 to β = 0.36); trait appearance comparison moderated in 6 of 8 studies. Body anxiety (2 studies, no effect), appearance self-esteem and body investment are single-study results. Text says 'four studies conducted a between subject, posttest only design' but names three posttest-only studies. Only 2 adolescent studies; no separate adolescent results. Quality text calls 40 studies 'high quality' though QCC ratings are positive/neutral/negative. Qi and Cui (2018) Study 1 and Study 2 counted separately within the 43. narrative_summary: Thematic synthesis of 13 qualitative studies of young people with lived ED experience: online ED content drove comparison (all 13 studies), which could trigger negative emotions and ED behaviours but felt more positive in recovery; young people curated content; online communities (11 of 13 studies) offered belonging and support but also harm, including pro-ED strategies.
narrative_locator: Discussion, Summary of findings and cross cutting themes (p. 12): 'Pro-ED communities had been experienced as helpful but also damaging by young people.'
author_conclusion: Online ED content is experienced as a double-edged sword, offering community and support but also triggering harm; young people lack supportive offline spaces; professionals should routinely explore online platforms' role in recovery, and digital literacy and co-designed interventions are needed.

primary_designs: Qualitative and quantitative primary studies; Table 2 labels all as qualitative except one quantitative questionnaire study (Ramsten et al. 2017)
narrative_summary: No study counts given. Across 17 Swedish studies, people with ID had limited internet access (less access to smartphones and computers, less online activity than non-disabled people), inaccessible design and digital-skill barriers, and restrictions set by staff and parents. People with ID viewed the internet positively; professionals were pessimistic. Wider interaction brought hate comments, threats and bullying.
narrative_locator: Results, 'The Swedish digital intellectual disability divide', Digital divide (p. 514): 'The articles showed that people with ID in Sweden have relatively limited access to the internet.'
author_conclusion: People with ID in Sweden have insufficient internet access; a digital disability divide and design and digital inequalities arise from societal structures, technology design and organisational conditions, not only impairment; equal, accessible support and national policy are needed.

narrative_summary: Narrative synthesis of 28 papers, mostly small or case studies. Cognition improved in 8 studies and memory in 6 with smartphone/tablet use. Barriers were mainly accessibility-related: motor impairments (8 studies), sensory impairments (7), device-specific complaints (6), difficulty learning (6), cognitive impairments (4); fear of technology addiction appeared in 1. People with dementia/ABI could learn and retain device use.
narrative_locator: Results, Barriers and Facilitators: 'The most frequently reported barriers to smartphone and tablet use ... pertained to the accessibility of the devices.'
author_conclusion: Smartphones and tablets can aid cognition (executive function, processing speed) with modest evidence for memory; users find them acceptable and nonstigmatizing, but use is hindered by digital literacy, unaccommodated motor and sensory impairments, and little clinician input; evidence is weak.

narrative_summary: Of 16 mostly descriptive studies (7 conference abstracts), 15 reported benefits of social media for people with TBI (social support in 11), 12 reported risks (Internet safety, e.g. cyberbullying, in 9; privacy in 6), and 10 reported barriers, including access problems and cognitive difficulties; none reported adverse events from social media use.

author_conclusion: Limited empirical, mostly descriptive evidence suggests social media offers people with TBI benefits for social participation and support, alongside online safety risks and cognitive and accessibility barriers; training and support for safe use and further rigorous research are needed.

extraction_notes: No meta-analysis; qualitative meta-synthesis with counts of studies per theme. Map cell 'PTSD and trauma' seems to reflect the word 'traumatic' in TBI; the review contains no PTSD or psychological trauma content. Counts left out to stay within 12 findings: convenience (8), information source (9), interactive communication (9), social connection (7), posting inappropriate content (5), cognitive rest (2), cognitive disability as barrier (5), behavioural disability as barrier (4), technical complexity (2), poor accessibility for visual deficits (2), health information (10). 'No adverse events' finding has estimate null because the paper states 'no' rather than a number. Focus counts overlap (12 user studies plus 5 content studies = 17 of 16). Participant numbers reported in 9 of 16 studies (range 8 to 155,101), so no total n. Duplicates removed before screening not counted in text. Outcomes outside the condition list (social isolation, social connection, satisfaction) not recorded.

online_exposures: online educational environments and educational media
population_notes: People with developmental dyslexia (acquired/organic dyslexia excluded); review states included studies had no strict age or gender restrictions; some studies also assessed teachers and parents; one study used students with low reading scores without a diagnosis; countries not reported
primary_designs: 30 quantitative (23 experimental, 7 questionnaire), 7 qualitative (case studies, interviews, documentary analysis)
narrative_summary: Of 37 studies (2017-2022), most treated poor online learning performance by dyslexic learners as a premise; several experiments/tests found lower online learning ability, plus reduced self-confidence, self-efficacy, stress and some anxiety/depression. 29 examined influencing factors (internal: impairment type, psychology; external: teachers, environment, media) and 18 interventions, mostly e-learning system development.
narrative_locator: Section 3.6 (p. 107): 'of the 37 papers covered in this article, 29 focused on exploring factors that influence the effectiveness of online learning for dyslexics'
author_conclusion: Dyslexia harms online learning: its comprehension- and task-based demands stress dyslexic learners and reduce self-efficacy and effectiveness; teachers, strategies, environments and media need adapting, and psychological interventions are a neglected research gap.

extraction_notes: No findings recorded: the counts reported (16 studies on effects of online learning, 28 on external factors, 14 on individual factors, 29 on influencing factors, 18 on interventions, 10 developing e-learning systems) describe study focus, not results with a direction, and results such as lower online learning ability are cited to studies without a stated count. Anxiety and depression are mentioned only from single studies (Soriano-Ferrer 2021; Hennessy 2022). Inconsistencies: methods say five years of literature, screening says six years 2017-2022, and the Scopus string includes 2023; eligibility lists Chinese, English or French but search strings limit to English; reviews excluded but WoS string includes Review Article. Map cell 'accessibility barriers': the review frames dyslexia as impairing online learning rather than platform accessibility as such. Outcomes outside the condition list (self-confidence, self-efficacy, stress, academic performance) not recorded.

narrative_summary: Of 20 studies, 10 addressed sexual, 8 financial and 2 criminal exploitation, without separating online from offline settings. Four studies identified intellectual disability as increasing the likelihood of sexual exploitation; 6 of 8 financial exploitation studies concerned older people with dementia or cognitive decline, which studies and practitioners framed as a vulnerability factor.
narrative_locator: Results, Study Design and Population: 'The types of exploitation reported included sexual ( n = 10), financial ( n = 8), and criminal ( n = 2) exploitation.'
author_conclusion: Cognitive impairment increases vulnerability to exploitation, but the relationship is not simple; few, disparate studies prevent conclusions about which impairments raise vulnerability to which exploitation types, and personal and societal factors also contribute.

extraction_notes: Exploitation is not specified as online; the only online element is Reid (2018), where chatting on the internet was an endangering circumstance for girls with intellectual disability. Fraud in Lichtenberg 2013/2016 is not specified as online. Map cells (scams and fraud; sexual exploitation and grooming) therefore rest on offline or unspecified exploitation. k = 10 used for the finding because that is the stated number of sexual exploitation studies; two further studies (Kenny 2020, Twill 2010) also examined intellectual disability with mental health. Depression and fraud (Lichtenberg 2013, 2016) not recorded because no count is stated. Single-study figures not recorded (4.86 times greater odds, Hestia 60%, Landers depression 62.3% and anxiety 51.2%). Errors: Discussion names Cole 2018 and Countryman-Roswurm and Bolin 2014 as financial exploitation studies, but Table 1 lists them as sexual exploitation; 'girls and young women (defined as those aged 25 years or older)' contradicts 'aged 25 or younger'; Cole cited as 2016 in text and 2018 in Table 1. Flow numbers (6,789 results; 222 duplicates; 495 non-empirical; 5,671 removed; 106 full texts) do not appear to reconcile.

online_exposures: stigma toward autism labels in online dating profiles
population_notes: Autistic adults in five participant studies (small convenience samples, average N = 16.6), one also including adults with mild ID; three studies on autistic males' dating profiles (52 public profiles; neurotypical female raters aged 18-57); UK, US and other English-speaking countries
primary_designs: 5 studies of dating app use by autistic people (interviews, observations, surveys, workshops; one dissertation), 3 quantitative profile studies (profile analysis, quasi-experimental, experimental); authors state all are cross-sectional
narrative_summary: Eight small, cross-sectional studies: five on autistic people's dating app use found a preference for online dating's control and pace but difficulties with dating norms and online-to-offline transition; safety concerns, higher online harassment and victimization, and unwanted sexual solicitation reported; three profile studies found autism labels rated more attractive except among high-stigma raters.
narrative_locator: Results, Characteristics of Included Records: 'While five of the included studies focused on the use of dating apps by autistic individuals, the other three examined how autistic males present themselves'
author_conclusion: Online dating offers autistic people a more controlled environment, but they face significant challenges with social norms, safety and self-presentation; evidence is small-sample and cross-sectional, with gaps on women, non-heterosexual people, preferences and autism-specific platforms.

online_exposures: information and communication technology (ICT) use for communication
population_notes: Autistic youth aged 10-17 years (9 studies) and adults (23 studies); underrepresented groups: autistic women, transgender, non-White, low-income, minimally speaking and/or with co-occurring intellectual disability
primary_designs: 19 quantitative, 12 qualitative, 1 mixed methods
narrative_summary: Abstract only: across 32 studies, three themes emerged: variation in ICT communication use; benefits (more control over online interaction, greater calm) and drawbacks (continued loneliness, desire for in-person friendships); and engagement in online autism communities that strengthen autistic identity. Quality ratings suggest an emergent evidence base. No study counts by result are available.
narrative_locator: Lay summary, 'What do these findings add': 'Some of the benefits of social media for autistic people include more control over how they talk and engage with others online'
author_conclusion: Evidence is emergent; exploring the positive social capital autistic people gain in online autism communities could support strengths-based interventions, while research is needed on sexuality and ICT to reduce online vulnerability, and on underrepresented groups.

extraction_notes: Treated as abstract only because the body of the article is behind a paywall in the file; the full text should be obtained. Abstract states five databases searched and PRISMA guidance; search date not given. The reference list in the file includes studies on cyberbullying victimization with depression and anxiety (Wright and Wachs 2019), internet addiction and ADHD symptoms (Kawabe 2019), internet addiction prevalence (So 2017) and gaming disorder (Paulus 2019), so the full text may hold results for counted conditions that could not be extracted here. Reference list also cites Harbour and Miller 2001 (grading system), possibly the quality tool, not confirmed. Loneliness (outside the condition list) reported as a drawback; not recorded.

online_exposures: web accessibility barriers (websites, web apps, web-based tools)
population_notes: People with cognitive disabilities aged 9 years and older, no upper age limit; any country, with preference in supplementary searches for EU studies and Greece, Ireland, Portugal and the UK; most frequent specific groups dyslexia, memory issues (dementia, aging, concussion) and autism
primary_designs: 31 qualitative, mixed methods or quasi-experimental; 14 experimental
narrative_summary: Across 45 studies (31 testing web tools: 14 novel, 17 existing), most reported barriers rather than supports: text-heavy sites, cognitive load when searching and verifying results, login and CAPTCHA problems, and exclusionary social media. Audio, video and picture formats helped people with dementia or concussion; autistic users benefited from limited scrolling. Few studies convincingly tested intervention success.
narrative_locator: Section 6.4: 'Overwhelmingly, the studies reviewed presented barriers or constraints for web accessibility. Less frequently, drivers or supports for web accessibility were discussed.'
author_conclusion: Web accessibility for people with cognitive disabilities remains fraught with barriers, chiefly text-based design and exclusion of these users from design; research needs real-world, co-designed, phased approaches, and the review proposes best practices.
rob_tool_used: CASP qualitative checklist (applied to all 45 studies, including the 14 experimental studies)

critical_flaws: 7: no list of excluded studies (PRISMA-P chart and general reasons only)

No findings recorded: counts reported (31 studies investigating web tools, 14 novel, 17 existing; 40% broad web accessibility vs 60% specific areas) describe study focus, not results with a direction; cross-study statements on barriers cite study groups without counts. Three existing tools were very poorly rated by users, each in a single study. Table 1 allows grey literature but searches were restricted to peer-reviewed results. Text refers to 'WCAG 1.9', apparently an error. Outcomes outside the condition list (frustration, self-concept, wellbeing) not recorded.

narrative_summary: Two of 25 studies reported past cyberbullying of adults with intellectual disabilities (one found no difference from other groups); other studies reported bullying, financial and sexual exploitation, timing unclear. Access barriers: inaccessible platform design (4 studies), lacking technical skills (6), cost; accessible design and co-design helped (3). Some users self-managed exploitation risks.
narrative_locator: Sections 6.3.1 and 6.3.3: 'Begara Iglesias et al. (2019) qualified this finding by saying that there were no differences in the frequency of experiences of cyberbullying'
author_conclusion: Adults with intellectual disabilities use social media with positive outcomes (inclusion, self-worth) and some negatives (bullying, exploitation); cost and design limit access. Some users self-manage risks; supporters need skills balancing autonomy and safety; research on severe disabilities needed.

amstar2.notes: Item 3 Y because the scoping design is used to justify including qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods research. Item 4 PY: 7 databases, search terms by four domains, reference lists and journal handsearching, but peer-reviewed English-language only without justification for language, no grey literature or expert contact, no search date. Item 5 N: title/abstract screening by three researchers independently, but full texts split one-third each and decided by one researcher (only 10 uncertain papers reviewed jointly). Item 8 Y: Appendix 1 gives aim, population, method, findings, platforms per study. Item 14 Y: authors discuss differing findings (e.g. Chiner vs Begara Iglesias) and sample composition (mild ID, wealthier countries).

funding: not reported for the review (acknowledgement only: open access publishing facilitated by La Trobe University via the Wiley - La Trobe University agreement through the Council of Australian University Librarians)
conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
extraction_notes: Scoping review, narrative synthesis, no pooled estimates. k for all count findings set to 25 (total included) because the review gives no per-question denominator. Cost barrier: Discussion says 'three of the studies' but cites only two (Heitplatz 2021; Sallafranque-St Louis & Normand 2017); Results 6.3.3 names the same two without a number; 3 recorded as printed. Sexual and financial exploitation: 'A number of other papers' (three cited: Lough & Fisher 2016; Shpigelman 2017; Shpigelman & Gill 2014) reported bullying, financial and sexual exploitation and social rejection, with no printed count and unclear whether incidents occurred; kept in narrative only. Single-study figures not recorded: Jenaro 2018b 15% experienced online bullying, associated with higher depression scores (depression is a counted condition); Jenaro 2018a overuse associated with drinking, smoking and gambling; Chiner 2017 all participants had negative online experiences (insults, threats, unwanted sexual photographs); Patrick 2020 13.2% used social media. Not recorded (perceptions rather than harms or access barriers): staff risk perceptions (6 studies), carer concerns about literacy and netiquette (5 papers), carers believing disability prevents use (3 studies), family support as facilitator (2 studies). Outcomes outside the condition list (disappointment, loneliness, social isolation in 3 studies; well-being, self-worth, self-esteem) not recorded. Paper errors: text says 14 countries but names 11; PRISMA figures (555 identified, 37 duplicates, 522 remaining) do not reconcile; Jenaro cited as '2108a/2108b'; Facebook said to be named in '13 papers' but more citations listed; Appendix 1 row for Patrick et al. (2020) lacks author/country label and Williams (2019) row columns are misaligned. Map cell 'Disability general' not separately addressed; review is ID-specific.

findings.label: Telephone and video contact usable and enjoyed by people with severe intellectual and multiple disabilities when given adapted microswitch technology and intensive training: 3 studies
findings.online_side: ICT-mediated social contact (telephone, video) via adapted microswitch technology (accessibility)
findings.locator: Section 4.2 Implications and directions for future studies: 'Three studies included in this review suggested that even people with severe intellectual and multiple disabilities could enjoy using the telephone'

narrative_summary: Nine studies, all on people with intellectual or multiple disabilities in care settings. Mild-to-moderate ID: mainstream ICT used, with practical and literacy barriers (account setup, jargon, typing, technical problems). Severe multiple disabilities: telephone and video usable only with adapted microswitch technology and intensive training (3 studies). Staff/family support often lacking; well-being evidence mixed, descriptive, high risk of bias.
narrative_locator: Section 4 Discussion: 'Reported barriers were practical (e.g., difficulties using a device) or cognitive in nature (e.g., literacy problems, understanding jargon).'
author_conclusion: Virtual social contact may be feasible and enjoyable for people with varied disabilities in care facilities, but evidence is scarce on whether it meets needs or affects well-being; more evidence needed before recommending it replace in-person contact.
rob_tool_used: Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT; Hong et al., 2018), two independent reviewers

amstar2.notes: Item 1 Y: eligibility stated in PICO format. Item 2 Y: PROSPERO CRD42020186442 plus OSF search protocol; deviations (dropped restricted-visiting criterion, dropped comparator search terms, abandoned well-being under restriction focus) explained. Item 4 PY: 5 databases, search protocol on OSF, published and unpublished studies sought, reference lists screened, last search 15 January 2021; no expert contact and English/Dutch/German limit not justified. Item 5 Y is a judgment call: titles/abstracts screened independently by two reviewers, full texts assessed by one reviewer, final selection by consensus of two. funding: Wellcome Trust Doctoral Studentship to Lianne Bakkum [208155/Z/17/Z]; ZonMw [641001101], [641001103], [641001104], [641001105] (Academische Werkplaatsen) and [10430022010013] (Project Digitaal op bezoek bij mensen met beperkingen)
extraction_notes: Narrative thematic synthesis; authors state only four of nine studies had quantitative findings, insufficient for quantitative synthesis. Only one cross-study count relevant to the map cell (accessibility) was recorded; other barrier statements give no counts. Eligibility covered motor disability, autism, visual and auditory impairment, deaf-blindness, acquired brain injury and multiple disability, but all included studies targeted intellectual disability. Outcomes outside the condition list (well-being, quality of life, loneliness, happiness/smiling, stress, frustration, quality of interpersonal relationships) not recorded. Single-study figures not recorded: Shpigelman & Gill (2014) 82% more comfortable talking on Facebook, 74% not feeling like everyone else, 88% did not enjoy using Facebook (the 88% sits uneasily with the positive experiences the review reports for the same study; worth checking against the primary paper); microswitch device cost about 2.000 US dollars. Perceived online risks (harassment, fraud victimisation, circulation of personal information) come from one study of staff perceptions (Ramsten et al., 2019) only. Title/abstract agreement reported as '55% (kappa = 0.547)'. Search window: studies published until May 2020, last search 15 January 2021.

narrative_summary: No study counts given. Table 5 states lower deliberative processing, reduced analytical reasoning and age-related cognitive decline consistently increase older adults' susceptibility to online health misinformation. critical_flaws: 7: no list of excluded studies with reasons; only 12 post-eligibility exclusions are named in the text, full-text exclusions are not itemized
9: no risk of bias or quality tool applied to the primary studies
noncritical_weaknesses: 3: no explanation of the choice of study designs for inclusion
10: funding sources of included studies not reported
12: impact of risk of bias on pooled results not assessed (only a measure-quality moderator analysis for cybervictimization)
amstar2.notes: 1: PECO components present, comparator implicit. 2: PROSPERO CRD42020182002 pre-registered; deviations not addressed, so PY. 4: PsycINFO, MedLine, CINAHL, full search string, reference lists of prior reviews; no grey literature; English-language and peer-reviewed restriction not justified (a strict AMSTAR 2 reading could give N; rated PY per rules v1.1 wording). 11: random effects justified, OR metric, I2 for cybervictimization only; some pools rest on k = 1 or 2 effects. 13: no formal risk of bias assessment, but discussion weighs self-report, cross-sectional designs, measure quality and unstable k < 3 estimates, so PY. 15: funnel plot, trim-and-fill and Egger for cybervictimization with ideation, plans and attempts; too few effects for other constructs.

extraction_notes: Source is the PMC author manuscript; the file still contains the reference list and PMC page text; the screening abstract field is '(none)'; supplementary docx not available. Cap: the review gives 21 main pooled estimates (Table 2) plus sub-level and subgroup estimates. Kept the 12 Table 2 estimates for the map-cell pairings (cybervictimization x4, cyberbullying perpetration x3, SITB-related social media use x4, problematic use x1). Left out, values as printed: Frequency of social media use (null): SI OR 1.45 (0.95-2.23, k 6, N 2,974, p .089); plans 1.47 (0.33-6.43, k 2, N 391, p .612); NSSI 2.03 (0.79-5.21, k 3, N 570, p .143); no data on attempts. Sexting: SI 2.37 (0.98-5.73, k 2, N 586, p .057); attempts 4.24 (3.13-5.44, k 1, N 11,707, p <.001); NSSI 3.07 (2.53-3.74, k 2, N 6,103, p <.001). Importance of social media: SI 1.05 (0.96-1.15, k 3, N 858, p .291); plans 1.02 (0.71-1.49, k 2, N 391, p .902); NSSI 1.25 (1.06-1.47, k 2, N 391, p .007). Sub-levels of SITB-related use (Results text only, no N): exposure to SITB content SI 2.12 (1.31, 3.43; k 3), plans 2.28 (1.99, 2.61; k 2), attempts 2.93 (1.96, 4.39; k 3), NSSI 3.13 (1.41, 6.96; k 1); generating/posting SITB content SI 3.96 (2.75, 5.71; k 3), plans 5.95 (2.27, 15.55; k 2), attempts 4.59 (1.83, 11.53; k 3), NSSI 2.45 (0.49, 12.37; k 1). The exposure-only sub-level is the closest match to the harmful content exposure map cell. Required subgroups also left out because of the cap (Table 3): cybervictimization-SI by age, adolescent OR 3.54 (2.98-4.20, k 29, p <.001) vs adult 1.69 (1.36-2.11, k 8, p <.001), moderator p <.001; cybervictimization-attempts by sample type, community 3.63 (2.66-4.97, k 22) vs at-risk or clinical 2.01 (1.83-2.22, k 3), moderator p .001. Age subgroups not run for attempts (only one adult study) and sample type not run for SI (only one clinical/at-risk study). Sensitivity without the Sueki et al. (2015) outlier effects: SITB-related use attempts 2.92 (1.78, 4.78), plans 2.64 (1.89, 3.68); posting SITB content plans 2.96 (2.53, 3.46), attempts 2.81 (1.11, 7.14). Striking moderators not recorded: cybervictimization-SI stronger with cybervictimization time frame > 3 months and SI time frame <= 1 year. k in Table 2 is the number of unique effects, not studies; authors call k < 3 estimates unstable. All pooled associations are cross-sectional; direction coded from the review's predictor (social media) to outcome (SITB) framing, not causal. Heterogeneity computed only for cybervictimization. n_participants_total not reported. Errors in paper: Results says too few effects '( k = 10 and k = 3, respectively)' for NSSI and suicide plans, which reverses Table 2 (plans k 10, NSSI k 3); Table 1 note defines 'SI = suicide attempt(s)' (should be SA); exposure-SI CI printed as '95% OR 1.31, 3.43'; Table 3 percentage-female row for attempts prints SE as '-0.01'; attempts I2 printed without % sign. No outcomes outside the condition list were analyzed.

narrative_summary: Abstract only. Four meta-analyses (three experimental, one longitudinal) all found negative effects of social media exposure on body image; experimental effects were smaller but still significant with outliers removed; no significant moderators emerged.
narrative_locator: Abstract: "These effects were smaller but significant with outliers removed." and "No significant moderators emerged."
author_conclusion: Appearance-ideal social media images worsen body image in experiments and social media use shows a very small negative longitudinal association; clinicians should address social media use and appearance-ideal exposure in case conceptualisation and psychoeducation.
rob_tool_used: none reported (abstract only)

amstar2.notes: Only the abstract is available.

extraction_notes: Abstract only. k values are samples, not studies; no total number of included studies or participants is given and the four analyses may share studies, so totals left null. No CIs, I2, model or publication bias results in the abstract. Negative g indicates worse body image after appearance-ideal exposure. Effects were 'smaller but significant with outliers removed' (no numbers given). Longitudinal effect printed as Fisher's Z and not converted; direction of the longitudinal analysis (use predicting later body image or the reverse) not stated in the abstract.
